title: Input and output: cout and cin

visuals.title: How data flows through a program

stages.detail: The user types a value and presses Enter.

visuals.title: Match each symbol to its job

pairs.meaning: Console output: sends data to the screen
Console input: reads data from the keyboard
Moves to a new line (and flushes the output)
Escape sequence for a new line inside a string

goal: After this you can print text and values with cout, read values from the keyboard with cin, and use endl, \n and chaining.
warmup: Imagine ordering at a canteen counter. The cashier asks, 'Which item?' (output), you say 'Samosa, 2 pieces' (input), and then the cashier tells you the bill (output). A program does the same: it shows a message with cout, waits for you to type with cin, and then shows a result with cout.
definition: cout (console output) sends text and values to the screen using the insertion operator <<. cin (console input) reads values typed on the keyboard into variables using the extraction operator >>. Both need #include <iostream>. The arrows show the direction of the data: << points towards cout (data goes out), >> points away from cin into the variable (data comes in).
howItWorks: Press Play on the Visualize tab. When the program reaches cin, it waits for the user. The typed value is placed in the variable box. cout then prints text and the current values of variables. You can chain many items in one statement: cout << a << b; or cin >> a >> b; The user separates the typed values with a space or Enter. cin >> on a string reads only one word, it stops at the first space.
syntax:
cout << "text";              // print text
cout << x;                    // print the value of x
cout << "x = " << x << endl;  // chain items, then new line
cout << "Line1\nLine2";       // \n also makes a new line
cout << "A\tB";               // \t is a tab

cin >> x;                     // read one value into x
cin >> a >> b;                // read two values (space or Enter between)
cin >> name;                  // string: reads one word only

sample.expectedOutput: Enter first number: Enter second number: Sum = 20

explanation.text: Declares three int variables in one line.
Shows a prompt so the user knows what to type.
Waits for the user and stores the typed number in a.
Prompt for the second number.

Adds a and b and stores the result in sum.

The prompt is printed (no new line, so the user types on the same line).
cin waits. The user types 12 and it goes into a.
The user types 8 and it goes into b.
Prints the result and a new line.

mistakes.error: no match for 'operator<<' (operand types are 'std::istream' and 'int'). cin uses >>
no match for 'operator>>' (operand types are 'std::ostream' and 'const char [3]'). cout uses <<
expected ';' before string constant (the << is missing)

mistakes.wrong:
string name;
cin >> name;   // user types: Ali Khan
mistakes.right: // cin >> name reads only Ali; use getline(cin, name) later for a full line
mistakes.error: no compiler error, but name holds only "Ali"; Khan is left unread

examTips: cout uses <<, cin uses >>. The arrows point in the direction the data moves.
Always print a prompt before cin so the user knows what to type.
endl and \n both give a new line. \t gives a tab. \\ prints a backslash and \" prints a double quote.
cin >> on a string stops at the first space, so it reads one word only.
Without #include <iostream>, neither cout nor cin works.
romanSummary: cout screen par output dikhata hai aur << (insertion operator) use karta hai.
cin keyboard se input leta hai aur >> (extraction operator) use karta hai.
Ek saath kai values: cin >> a >> b; aur cout << a << b;
\n ya endl nayi line ke liye hai, \t tab ke liye.
string par cin >> sirf ek word parhta hai, space aate hi ruk jata hai.
